label: <DEL> step, when the sequence has many h/i/p/g/u/o/j/digit tokens and few w/s/e/z/k/y/b/d/t/r
explanation: Almost entirely a delimiter-step unit: 90% of activations and 93.5% of activation mass are at the <DEL> step (t == L), but it fires on only 11% of <DEL> steps. Which <DEL> steps fire depends on the content of the whole original sequence, spread across many tokens. h, i, p, g, u, o, j and digits push it up (top examples look like p 3 i h h, p i i i, 1 i 2 h), with h strongest, especially as the last or second-to-last token, and next_out == i (original token 1 is i) at 7x lift. w, s, e, z, k, y, b, d, t, r suppress it. A balance count (positive tokens minus suppressing tokens >= 2) gets dev F1 0.45 and mass recall 0.80. Thresholding a weighted count does not separate it much better, so the selection looks like a distributed linear readout of the sequence content. Activation is larger when the balance is more extreme, e.g. sequences made almost only of h/i/digits/p; this was seen in the examples, not measured. It rarely fires in the original phase (5% of mass, mostly on w/s/e/z/k inputs that come after h/i-heavy prefixes) and almost never in the copy phase (1.5%).

scorecard.summary: Graded preference over the third original token (most: i, h, 2, p, 3, 1; least: t, s, e, w) and the next token to output (most: i, p, o, u, 3, 2; least: e, s, w, z); timing cues that raise it most: phase=1, recall_idx=0, t=4.
